extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent practitioners, and patent examiners handling 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits/declarations (pre‑AIA matters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and evaluating affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 to antedate references under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103, covering who may sign, formalities, evidentiary showing (conception, reduction to practice, diligence), dates, geographic limits, and interplay with patents/publications claiming the same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may make affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 to overcome a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 must be made by either: (A) the entire inventive entity (the inventor); (B) less than all named joint inventors if shown that they invented the subject matter of the claim(s) under rejection; (C) for applications filed before Sept. 16, 2012, a joint inventor or assignee under pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.47 if a petition was granted or the application was accepted under pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.42 or 1.43; (D) for pre‑Sept. 16, 2012 applications, the legal representative of a deceased, insane or legally incapacitated sole inventor or joint inventor where applicable under pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.42 or 1.43; (E) for applications filed on or after Sept. 16, 2012, the party qualified under 37 CFR 1.42 or 1.46; (F) the assignee or other party in interest when it is not possible to produce the affidavit/declaration of the (joint) inventor; (G) the owner of the patent under reexamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one or more named joint inventors originally signed the oath/declaration but later are unavailable for a 1.131(a) affidavit in pre‑Sept. 16, 2012 applications, remaining joint inventors may sign if a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 requesting waiver of the unavailable inventor's signature is submitted along with proof of unavailability (similar to petition under pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.47). Petitions under 1.183 are decided by the Office of Petitions (MPEP §1002.02(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements of affidavits and declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit is a written statement under oath before a notary or authorized officer; 37 CFR 1.68 permits use of a declaration instead. The declaration must include an acknowledgment that willful false statements are punishable under 18 U.S.C. 1001 and may jeopardize the application/patent. The declarant must state that statements of their own knowledge are true and statements on information and belief are believed to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §602 et seq. for additional formal affidavit requirements. Ensure the declaration contains the required criminal‑false‑statement acknowledgment and the appropriate language distinguishing knowledge vs information/belief. Treat declarations as equivalent to affidavits for Rule 131 practice where permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of U.S. patent or application publication claiming same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: For pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 applications: if a noncommonly owned U.S. patent or published application claims the same invention and its publication/issue date is less than 1 year prior to presentation of claims in the examined application, the applicant's remedy (if any) must be by interference under 37 CFR 41.202 rather than by a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit. If a U.S. patent issues more than 1 year prior to presentation of claims, a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(1) should be made. If a published application (35 U.S.C. 122(b) or certain WIPO PCT publications) published more than 1 year prior to presentation, a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(2) may be appropriate if the examined application was filed after the publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note such facts in the Office action and use the appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., ¶¶23.14, 23.14.01). A 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit is ineffective to overcome a U.S. patent or publication not only when claims are verbatim but also when there is no patentable distinction; identical or non‑patentably distinct claims constitute 'interfering subject matter' (37 CFR 41.203(a)) and cannot be overcome by a Rule 131(a) affidavit. For commonly owned references where claims are not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) may be used to overcome a pre‑AIA 103 rejection (see MPEP §718).

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts and documentary evidence required to establish priority
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential showing under 37 CFR 1.131(a) is priority of invention by satisfactory evidence of FACTS, not mere conclusions. Exhibits may accompany the affidavit/declaration and each exhibit relied upon should be specifically referred to in terms of what it is relied upon to show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible supporting exhibits include attached sketches, blueprints, photographs, reproductions of notebook entries, models, supporting witness statements (for verbal disclosures), testimony from an interference (with specific parts pointed out), and documents from the Disclosure Document Program (where applicable historically). Exhibits and models must comply with 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into the file. Each exhibit need not support all claimed limitations provided missing limitations are supported by the affidavit/declaration itself. General, vague allegations or conclusory statements describing exhibits without specifics are insufficient (see In re Borkowski, In re Harry). Cite specific parts of exhibits and explain exactly what facts they establish and when.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for original exhibits or explanation when absent (37 CFR 1.131(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.131(b) requires that original exhibits of drawings or records, or photocopies thereof, accompany and form part of the affidavit/declaration, or their absence be satisfactorily explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If original sketches/models are lost, reproduce and furnish them or state their contents as precisely as possible; if relying on verbal disclosures, the witness should recite as nearly as possible the language used. The examiner must consider the affidavit/declaration and all accompanying exhibits, records and notes in their entirety when evaluating a Rule 131 submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of dates in affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: When alleging conception or reduction to practice prior to a reference, dates in the oath/declaration may be the actual dates or, if disclosure of actual dates is not desired, the declarant may allege that the acts occurred prior to a specified date. However, the actual dates of acts relied upon to establish diligence must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exhibit dates have been removed or blocked, the matter of dates can be addressed in the body of the affidavit/declaration. Diligence acts require actual dates (see MPEP §715.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three ways to show prior invention under 37 CFR 1.131(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 CFR 1.131(b) applicant can establish prior invention by one of three showings: (A) actual reduction to practice of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference; (B) conception prior to the effective date of the reference coupled with due diligence from prior to the reference date to a subsequent actual reduction to practice; or (C) conception prior to the effective date of the reference coupled with due diligence from prior to the reference date to the filing date of the application (constructive reduction to practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception must be followed by reasonable diligence to some other act (actual reduction or filing). Some simple devices may require only mere construction to constitute reduction to practice; proof of actual working apparatus and utility may be required depending on facts. Where reduction to practice has not occurred before the reference, diligence must be continuous from just prior to the reference up to actual reduction or filing. See MPEP §2138.04‑.06 for fuller discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception, reduction to practice, utility, and corroboration nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms 'conception,' 'reasonable diligence,' and 'reduction to practice' generally have the same meanings under Rule 131 as in interference proceedings, but Rule 131 practice is not strictly controlled by interference law. Conception is the mental part of invention and must be capable of proof (drawings, disclosure to another, etc.). Proof of reduction to practice generally requires showing an apparatus actually existed and worked for its intended purpose; for very simple devices mere construction may suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of utility is required only if the reference discloses a utility; whether test results are required depends on case facts — the ultimate question is whether one of ordinary skill would be satisfied to a reasonable certainty that the subject matter had the alleged utility. Unlike interference practice (which requires corroboration), averments in a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit/declaration do not require corroboration — an applicant may stand on their own affidavit/declaration if they choose (see Ex parte Hook). Nevertheless, case law (e.g., In re NTP) cautions that uncorroborated testimony may be insufficient in some contexts; be sure documentary support is provided where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence: timing, proof, and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence must be shown by evidence of facts establishing it; mere allegation of diligence is insufficient. Diligence comes into question only after prior conception is clearly established. The critical period for diligence begins just before the effective date of the reference and ends with the date of reduction to practice (actual or constructive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor is either diligent or not — there are no degrees; periods of inactivity can be excused but an explanation/justification must be on the record (the USPTO/courts will not speculate). Only diligence before reduction to practice matters; lack of diligence between an actual reduction and the filing date is irrelevant to Rule 131 sufficiency. Use form paragraph 7.62.fti where diligence is lacking. See MPEP §2138.06 for detailed discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of interference testimony as substitute evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony from an interference proceeding may sometimes be used in lieu of a Rule 131 affidavit/declaration to antedate a reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using interference testimony, the applicant must point out the specific part(s) of the testimony relied upon; examiners should not be required to search entire interference records for the evidence (see Ex parte Bowyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic limitation on acts relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts relied upon to show prior invention under 37 CFR 1.131(a) must have been carried out in the United States or in a NAFTA or WTO member country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §715.07(c) for applicability. Ensure all acts and supporting exhibits fall within the permitted jurisdictions when attempting to antedate a reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species vs. genus evidence and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where predictability is in question, showing prior completion of one or a few species within a disclosed genus is generally not sufficient to overcome the reference or activity. The test is whether the species completed by the inventor prior to the reference provided an adequate basis for inferring generic applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law examples: In small genera (e.g., halogens with four species), reduction to practice of three, or perhaps two, species might complete the generic invention; in genera of hundreds of species a considerably larger number of reductions to practice would probably be necessary (In re Shokal). The affidavit need not show the inventor viewed the invention as encompassing more than the species actually made; the question is whether the affidavit facts would persuade one of ordinary skill that the inventor possessed as much of the invention as shown in the reference.
